title: Diwali Rush Lifts Indian Food Exports as Global Buyers Stock Up on Sweets and Snacks
excerpt: A Trade Promotion Council of India survey of overseas buyers shows festive-season orders running about 6 percent above last year, with Gulf markets leading and ready-to-eat foods growing fastest.
body:
• A Trade Promotion Council of India survey of overseas buyers shows Diwali-season orders running about 6 percent above last year, with some markets up more than 15 percent.
  • Traditional festive staples — kaju katli, laddoo, halwa, bhujia, murukku, ghee and pickles — top procurement lists, while ready-to-eat and ready-to-cook foods are the fastest-growing segment.
  • Gulf markets (Kuwait, Oman, Bahrain) drive the seasonal rush; a German importer reported roughly 25 percent year-on-year growth in ready-to-eat imports.
  • India's ready-to-eat and cooked food exports rose 16 percent to $2.4 billion in FY2025-26, but exporters still face high freight costs, compliance hurdles and shipping-route risks.

Diwali orders pour in early for Indian food exporters

Indian food and beverage exporters are seeing a clear pickup in overseas orders ahead of Diwali, with international buyers reporting average demand growth of about 6 percent for the festive season and some markets recording increases above 15 percent, according to the Trade Promotion Council of India (TPCI).

The TPCI survey of overseas importers points to a stable-to-moderate expansion in festive procurement, led by traditional products — sweets, savories, rice, spices, pickles and ghee — while ready-to-eat and ready-to-cook foods are emerging as the fastest-growing segment. Frozen snacks, prepared meals, festive mixes, instant mixes, Indian breads, curries and cooked rice are moving in larger volumes than in previous years.

“Festive-season demand signals are encouraging for India's food and beverage exporters,” TPCI Chairman Mohit Singla said. “What is particularly significant is the combination of strong demand for traditional Indian products such as sweets, savories, rice, spices and pickles with the rapid emergence of ready-to-eat and ready-to-cook foods.”

Context & Background

India's mithai and namkeen industry, valued at about ₹1.5 lakh crore domestically, has been building export capacity for years. Roughly 10 percent of Indian sweets and namkeens now ship overseas, with shipments growing at more than 10 percent annually, Feroz H. Naqvi, Director-General of the Federation of Sweets and Namkeen Manufacturers, said at the World Mithai & Namkeen Convention in Hyderabad this July.

Packaging and shelf-life technology has unlocked the farthest markets. “We have been exporting sweets for many decades, but demand has increased considerably of late,” said Neeraj Agarwal, Director of Haldiram's. The Nagpur-based company ships to the United States, Canada, Singapore, Japan and Southeast Asia. Advances in preservation technology have let Indian sweets hold quality over long shipping times — a problem that once confined exports to nearby markets.

Capacity is being built specifically for exports. Hyderabad-based Dadu Mithai Vatika is commissioning a dedicated export kitchen for large-scale production of motichoor laddus for overseas buyers, according to Managing Director Rajesh Dadu, and is experimenting with chocolate-based sweets and dry-fruit combinations that are gaining popularity in the Gulf, the US and Europe.

“We have been exporting sweets for many decades, but demand has increased considerably of late.”

— Neeraj Agarwal, Director, Haldiram's

Impact & Analysis

The demand pattern points to a structural shift in who buys Indian food. The Gulf Cooperation Council markets — Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain — remain the strongest regional demand center, with Kuwait buyers procuring sweets, ghee, paneer, beverages, condiments, spices, pickles, canned foods and dry fruits. India's food and beverage exports to the United Arab Emirates alone rose from $2.3 billion in 2021 to $3.6 billion in 2025, an 11.3 percent compound annual rate, according to TPCI.

Europe is becoming the next phase of growth. A German importer reported about 25 percent year-on-year growth in ready-to-eat food imports, while a Kuwait buyer reported 28 percent growth, per the TPCI survey. European buyers are increasingly sourcing Indian convenience foods — frozen, organic, vegan and health-oriented categories — for mainstream retail and foodservice, not just ethnic aisles. That demand carries a price: tighter food-safety, labeling and import-compliance standards are pushing Indian suppliers toward better packaging, certification and cold-chain infrastructure.

It is not all tailwinds. TPCI flagged high freight and container costs, customs inspection delays, food-safety and compliance requirements, limited shelf life and geopolitical instability as persistent concerns. Disruptions to West Asian shipping routes are especially sensitive for exporters serving Gulf markets, where timely delivery of seasonal and perishable goods is non-negotiable.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian-origin families abroad, the export boom shows up directly on the Diwali table. Indian gulab jamun now ranks among the most popular desserts in the United Kingdom, Naqvi said, while rasgulla, soan papdi and Mysore pak are appearing on dessert menus far beyond South Asian neighborhoods. In the US, major retailers including Target, Walmart and Costco have begun stocking Diwali-specific foods and sweets, recognizing a market of nearly 4.4 million Indian Americans.

Gulf shoppers are driving a taste shift of their own: chocolate-based sweets and dry-fruit combinations, unfamiliar formats in traditional mithai, are gaining ground there and in Western markets. The result is a Diwali gift box that looks increasingly global — kaju katli and bhujia alongside roasted makhana assortments and fusion sweets, shipped from export kitchens built specifically to serve buyers thousands of miles from the factory.

What's Next

TPCI sees the festive season as a springboard rather than just a sales spike. “The festive season provides crucial momentum for our exporters to transition from traditional commodity exports toward building strong, recognized global brands in food sector,” Singla said, adding that while the Gulf remained the immediate growth driver, Europe offered the next phase of expansion.

India's exports of ready-to-eat and cooked food products reached $2.4 billion in the financial year ended March 2026, up 16 percent from $2.1 billion a year earlier. Whether that trajectory holds through the festival depends on execution — certification, shelf-life technology and logistics — as much as on demand. For now, the orders are in, and exporters have a narrow window before the festival to get them right.
